2027-07-13.title: Tuesday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Henry
readings: She named him Moses, “because I drew him out of the water”
You who seek God, let your hearts revive
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!
2027-07-13.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). From today the first reading follows the story of Moses, which runs through the weekdays of weeks 15 and 16. Optional memorial of St Henry, the emperor who ruled as a servant of the poor; the Mass is of the weekday unless the priest chooses the memorial. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. In Kerala the monsoon rivers are full this month, and the baby in the basket among the reeds is easy to picture. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-13.verse: When the child grew up, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and she took him as her son. She named him Moses, “because,” she said, “I drew him out of the water.”
theo: The book of Exodus opens with a people under pressure. Pharaoh has ordered every Hebrew boy to be thrown into the Nile, and today's reading begins with one family's answer. A man and a woman of the house of Levi have a son. His mother sees that he is “a fine baby” and hides him for three months. When she can hide him no longer she does a remarkable thing: she obeys Pharaoh's order, and defeats it. She does put the child in the Nile, but in a “papyrus basket” plastered with bitumen and pitch. The Hebrew word for this basket, tebah, is the word used for Noah's ark; the Bible is quietly telling us that another great rescue through water has begun. The child's sister, who is later named Miriam, stands at a distance and watches. Three women save him: the mother who lets go, the sister who keeps watch, and the daughter of Pharaoh who “took pity on him” although she knows at once that he is “one of the Hebrews’ children.” The tyrant's own house shelters the one who will break the tyrant's power, and the boy's mother is even paid wages to nurse her own son. Then comes the name: “She named him Moses, ‘because,’ she said, ‘I drew him out of the water.’” The name echoes the Hebrew for “to draw out.” The one drawn out of the water will draw a whole people out of the sea. The reading then jumps forward. Moses, grown up, sees an Egyptian beating one of his kinsfolk and kills him, and the next day one of his own people asks: “Who made you a ruler and judge over us?” Moses flees to Midian and sits down by a well. St Stephen will later say that Moses thought his people would understand that God was rescuing them through him, “but they did not understand,” and yet this very Moses was the one “whom God now sent as both ruler and liberator” (Acts 7:25, 35). The psalm is the prayer of a person in deep water: “I have come into deep waters, and the flood sweeps over me,” and yet “the Lord hears the needy.”

In the Gospel Jesus speaks hard words, and they have to be heard as words of grief. “Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his deeds of power had been done, because they did not repent.” The cities are Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, small towns around the Sea of Galilee. Capernaum was the base of his ministry, and Bethsaida was the town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). The cry “Woe to you!” is the cry of the prophets over a city they love; it is closer to a mourner's “Alas for you!” than to a curse. The reason is not that these towns were worse than others but that they had been given more. They had seen the deeds of power, the healings and the teaching, and had not repented, which in the Bible means turning round and changing direction. Jesus compares them with Tyre and Sidon, pagan harbour cities that the prophets had condemned, and even with Sodom, the byword for sin. If those cities had seen what you saw, he says, they would have repented “long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” On the day of judgment it will be “more tolerable” for them: grace that is received and not used becomes a weight. Jesus speaks here as a son of Israel to his own neighbours in Galilee, in the manner of the prophets, and the Gospels show that many from these very towns did follow him; the first disciples came from them. The words are a family's lament, not a verdict against a people. The two readings meet in one question. Moses was drawn out of the water, and his people did not at first know their deliverer. Jesus was among his people, and many of his towns had seen and not yet turned. What have we done with what we have been given: our baptism, the Word, the Mass? Nothing in the Gospel is said to make us anxious; it is said to wake us up while there is still time to turn.
outline: Ask: who held you up when you could not hold yourself, and have you ever thanked them?
Point 1 · Drawn out of the water
A mother, a sister and a princess save the child who will save a people.
Point 2 · Who made you a ruler?
The deliverer is not yet recognised; God's time is longer than ours.
Jesus laments over the towns that saw most and turned least: gifts bring responsibility.
Point 4 · St Henry, an emperor who served
A crown understood as a trust for the poor and for peace.
“Because I drew him out of the water.”
live: Find the date of your baptism, thank God for it, and sign yourself with holy water when you come into church or when you leave home today.
Count what you have been given (Matthew 11:21)

Write down five gifts of faith you have received, such as the Mass, the Bible, a praying grandmother or a good priest, and ask what you have done with each. Plan one act of turning back, perhaps confession.
saints: Born in Bavaria, he became King of Germany in 1002 and Holy Roman Emperor in 1014. With his wife Kunigunde, who is also a saint, he founded the diocese of Bamberg and supported monasteries and the renewal of Church life. He understood his crown as a trust from God for justice, for the poor and for peace, and he is remembered as an oblate of the Benedictines. He died on 13 July 1024 and was canonised in 1146.
2027-07-13.prayer: Lord God, you saw the cry of your people and drew Moses out of the water to be their deliverer. Draw us out of every flood that threatens to carry us away, and teach us to thank those who held us up when we could not hold ourselves. Lord Jesus, you grieved over the cities that saw your works and did not turn: give us hearts that are quick to repent and quick to be grateful. Through the intercession of St Henry, make all who hold power servants of the poor and makers of peace. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest pours a little water into the wine, and prays that we may share in the divinity of Christ who humbled himself to share our humanity. It is a small sign of baptism: we have been drawn out of the water. And the Mass is the greatest deed of power we shall ever see. The towns of Galilee saw healings; we see bread become his Body, and we are asked the same question as they were: will we turn to him? That is why the Mass begins with “Lord, have mercy.”

quick: A mother hides her baby, then places him in a basket on the Nile; the daughter of Pharaoh takes pity on him and names him Moses, “drawn out.”
Moses, grown up, defends a kinsman, kills an Egyptian, is rejected by his own people and flees to Midian.
Jesus grieves over Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, which saw most of his deeds of power and did not repent.
2027-07-13.action: Thank, by name or by letter or call, one person who held you up when you could not hold yourself.
2027-07-13.question: Do I treat the gifts of my faith as a treasure to use or only as something I already have?
kidsaint: Henry lived a thousand years ago in Germany and became a king and then an emperor. He did not want to be a king for his own glory. He wanted to look after poor people and to keep peace. He built churches and helped build a new diocese at a city called Bamberg. He prayed a great deal. His wife, Kunigunde, was a saint too. Henry teaches us that being strong means helping others.

family.explain: A mother loved her baby very much, but a bad king wanted to harm baby boys. She made a little basket, put her baby inside and placed it among the reeds at the river's edge. His big sister watched from far away. The king's daughter came to wash in the river, found the baby and felt sorry for him. She gave him a name: Moses, which means “drawn out of the water.” God was looking after him all the time, and when he grew up he led God's people to safety.
family.intention: We thank God for our parents, grandparents and everyone who has looked after us, and we pray for children who have no one to look after them.
family.ask: Ask: “Who helped to look after me when I was small? How can I say thank you this week?”

illus: In the floods of 2018 a young nurse near the Pamba river spent two nights on a rooftop with strangers. A fisherman's boat reached them and took her to a relief camp, and in the camp a stranger shared her only dry blanket with her. Years later the nurse could not recall the fisherman's name, but she could recall the blanket exactly. She said she now keeps one spare blanket in her car for anyone who needs it. We are all people who were once pulled out of the water by someone whose name we may not remember; and one day we will be asked whom we pulled out. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you hear the groaning of your people. Draw us out of the water, and make us grateful. Amen.
share: She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds (Exodus 2:3). Who placed me safely and watched from a distance when I was small or weak?
Who made you a ruler and judge over us? (Exodus 2:14). Has God ever sent me to help someone who did not welcome me, and how did I respond?
Woe to you, Chorazin! (Matthew 11:21). Which of the gifts God has given me have I begun to take for granted?
pm.resp: You who seek God, let your hearts revive.
interc: For the Church, that she may grieve over the world's sins with the heart of Jesus and not with anger.
For all who care for children who have been abandoned, and for those who adopt them.
For rulers and public servants, that like St Henry they may see power as a duty to the poor.
For victims of floods and the monsoon rains, and for those who rescue them.
For our group, that we may turn back to the Lord quickly and gratefully.
pm.close: Father, you drew Moses out of the water and sent him to deliver your people. Draw us to yourself, and let our lives be thanks for all that we have received. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, picture a river and a basket among the reeds. In the basket is a three-month-old baby. His mother has done everything she can; now she has to trust God. And God does what he so often does: he uses ordinary people. A mother who lets go, a sister who stands and watches, and a princess who does not look away from a crying baby. Look at how many small hands it takes to save one child. The woman who draws him out of the river names him Moses: because I drew him out of the water (Exodus 2:10). He will draw out a whole people.

We too have been drawn out of the water. In baptism, God lifted us out of the old life and gave us a name. Who were the hands that held you? A mother, a grandmother, a teacher, a priest, a neighbour. Today is a good day to remember them and to thank God for them, and to ask: whom am I holding up?

The story goes on. Moses grows up, sees his people suffering, and tries to help in his own way, with violence, and it goes badly. His own people say: Who made you a ruler and judge over us? (Exodus 2:14). He runs away. It looks like the end, but it is only the beginning: forty years later God will send this same Moses from a burning bush. God's time is longer than ours. When our own good plans fail, God has not stopped.

In the Gospel Jesus grieves over three towns. Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! (Matthew 11:21). It sounds harsh, but listen to the heart behind it: it is the cry of a friend who has done everything and sees his friends still not turning. They saw the most miracles and changed the least. How much have we seen? The Mass every Sunday, the Bible in our own language, the sacraments, the saints. St Henry, whom we remember today, was an emperor who knew that much had been given to him, and so much would be asked. Let us turn back with gratitude today, and let us not wait. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago a baby was in great danger. His mother made a little basket, put him inside it and placed it by the river. His big sister watched to see what would happen. Then a king's daughter came, found the baby and loved him. She called him Moses, which means “drawn out of the water.” Moses grew up and became a great helper of God's people. God uses many people to look after one child: a mother, a sister and a princess. Who looked after you? Let us say thank you to them today, and let us look after someone smaller too.

intro: Theme: “I drew him out of the water.”
A basket among the reeds, a deliverer not yet recognised, and the Lord's grief over the towns that saw most and turned least.

q: When the child grew up, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and she took him as her son. She named him Moses, “because,” she said, “I drew him out of the water.”
By faith Moses was hidden by his parents for three months after his birth, because they saw that the child was beautiful; and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.
points.apply: Thank, today, one person who held you up when you could not hold yourself, and ask whom you are holding up.

sub: God's time is longer than ours.
q: He answered, “Who made you a ruler and judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?”
“It was this Moses whom they rejected when they said, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’ and whom God now sent as both ruler and liberator through the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
points.apply: Where a good plan of yours has failed, hand it to God again this week and ask what he wants to do with it.

sub: A prophet's lament, not a curse.
q: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord God, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
points.apply: Go to confession this week, and begin the examination of conscience with the question: what have I been given?

sub: Bamberg, and the poor at his table.
q: If a king judges the poor with equity, his throne will be established forever.

It will not be so among you; but whoever wishes to be great among you must be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you must be your slave; just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.
points.apply: Whatever authority you have, at home, at work or in the parish, ask this week how you can use it for the weakest person under it.

concl: God draws Moses out of the water by the hands of three women, and uses a rejected deliverer in his own good time.
Jesus grieves over the towns that received most; the answer to his lament is not fear but a quick, grateful turning back.
2027-07-13.resolve: Thank one person who held you up, and take one concrete step of turning back to the Lord this week.
